title: Evaluation of Tilt-correction of Anteversion on Anteroposterior Pelvic Radiographs in Total Hip Arthroplasty
question: Can the Tannast symphococcygeal distance method correct acetabular cup anteversion for pelvic tilt on routine post-operative radiographs after hip arthroplasty?

bottom_line.question: Can the Tannast symphococcygeal distance method correct acetabular cup anteversion for pelvic tilt on routine post-operative radiographs after hip arthroplasty?
bottom_line.answer: The correction could not be applied to 44% of radiographs, and where it was applied, corrected anteversion correlated very poorly with intraoperative navigation (r = -0.07), so the authors judge the method unsuitable for patients having hip arthroplasty.

provenance.quote: The correction method could not be applied in 44% (31/71) of the cases, chiefly due to difficulties in visualizing the required landmarks. In cases where it could be applied, corrected values correlated very poorly with navigation measurements (r = -0.07).

sections.title: Why Cup Angle Matters and How Pelvic Tilt Distorts X-rays
sections.markdown:
After a total hip replacement (total hip arthroplasty, or THA), surgeons check how the new hip socket was placed. The socket is a cup fixed into the pelvis. If it sits at the wrong angle, the hip wears out faster, the implant can loosen, movement is more limited, and impingement and dislocation become more likely.

Two angles describe the cup. Inclination is how steeply it tips upward and outward. **Anteversion** is how far it faces forward. The standard way to check both is a front-to-back (anteroposterior, or AP) X-ray of the pelvis. X-rays are cheap, easy to get and use little radiation. The problem is that an X-ray flattens a three-dimensional pelvis into a flat picture, and the way the patient lies or stands changes that picture.

The main source of error is **pelvic tilt**, which is how far the pelvis rocks forward or backward relative to the X-ray plate. Tilt barely affects inclination. Anteversion is different, because it is read entirely from the shape of the oval that the cup's rim makes on the film, and tilting the pelvis changes that oval directly. The same cup can look more or less anteverted depending on the patient's posture.

sections.title: The Method Being Tested
sections.markdown:
Several ways to correct for tilt have been proposed, but none is in routine clinical use. One widely cited method, from Tannast and colleagues, uses the **symphococcygeal distance (SCD)**. This is the vertical distance on the X-ray between the top of the pubic symphysis (the joint at the front of the pelvis) and the sacrococcygeal joint (where the tailbone meets the sacrum). They found that this distance tracks pelvic tilt well. They then published nomograms, which are lookup charts with separate versions for men and women. You enter the SCD and the measured anteversion, and the chart returns a "tilt-corrected" anteversion.

There are two reasons to doubt that the method carries over to hip replacement patients. Tannast's X-rays were taken under strict conditions that differ from routine practice. Their patients were also young (mean age 31.7) and had impingement or hip dysplasia, while hip replacement patients are older. The authors here tested whether the method works on ordinary post-operative X-rays in THA patients.

sections.title: How They Tested It
sections.markdown:
This was a retrospective study at one centre. It covered patients who had a first or repeat hip replacement by one surgeon between February 2016 and February 2017. During each operation the surgeon used the Intellijoint HIP navigation system. A camera is pinned to the pelvis and records the pelvis's orientation at the start of surgery. Because the camera stays fixed to the patient, its anteversion reading reflects the cup's true position in the body and is unaffected by imaging or by the pelvis shifting on the table. The study used it as the reference value.

Two weeks after surgery, patients had standing AP X-rays. Each image was scaled using the known size of the implanted femoral head. One researcher, who did not know the navigation values, measured anteversion and the SCD three times per image, averaged the results, and applied Tannast's nomograms. That gave three numbers per hip: uncorrected X-ray, corrected X-ray, and navigation.

Agreement was measured with Pearson's r, which runs from 1 (two measures move together perfectly) through 0 (no relationship) to -1 (they move in opposite directions).

sections.title: What They Found
sections.markdown:
Of 77 eligible cases, 6 were excluded (one pelvic fracture, five X-rays too poor to measure), leaving 71.

- The tailbone joint could not be seen on 31 of the 71 X-rays (44%).
- Of the remaining 40, 9 (23%) gave measurements outside the range the nomograms cover.
- The paper reports that the correction could be applied to only 31 of 71 cases. However, its comparisons describe a "correction-eligible" group of 40, so the counts do not fully line up.

Measurement consistency was excellent. Repeat measurements agreed almost perfectly (intraclass correlation 0.99 for both anteversion and SCD), so the problems below do not come from an unsteady measurer.

In the correction-eligible group, average anteversion was:

- Uncorrected X-ray: 25.2° (SD 7.6°)
- Navigation: 27.4° (SD 5.7°)
- Corrected X-ray: 36.9° (SD 7.4°)

The correction raised anteversion in every case, by an average of 13.5° (p<0.001). Corrected values differed from navigation by an average of 10.8°. The correlation between corrected and navigation values was r = -0.07, which means essentially no relationship. Corrected values did track the uncorrected ones (r = 0.73). In other words, the correction mostly pushed every reading upward by a similar amount, without responding to each patient's actual tilt.

The uncorrected X-ray also correlated weakly with navigation (r = 0.15), but it came much closer on average:

mean difference = uncorrected minus navigated = -2.2°

The standard deviation of that difference was 8.7°, and the two sets of values did not differ significantly (p=0.16). For all its known flaws, the raw X-ray landed closer to the navigation value than the corrected one did.

sections.title: Why It Matters
sections.markdown:
The upward bias carries a clinical risk. If corrected values read too high, a surgeon may conclude the cup has more forward tilt than it does and aim for less. Low anteversion is a risk factor for posterior dislocation, where the hip slips out backward.

The authors give several possible reasons the method failed here:

- **Imaging setup.** Tannast used a fixed 1.2 m distance between the X-ray source and the plate, patients lying down, and a specific beam target. Routine post-operative images are taken lying or standing, with the beam aimed at the pubic symphysis and small variations in distance.
- **Patients.** The THA patients averaged 63.1 years old, and their anatomy differs from that of Tannast's younger group.
- **Measurement details.** Tannast did not say whether "vertical" was measured relative to the pelvis or to the X-ray frame, or how images were scaled. Magnification matters here. Software usually assumes 115% to 120%, but actual magnification ranges from 97% to 127%.

The study has limits. It was retrospective, so X-ray technique varied between patients. It also compares X-rays taken after surgery with navigation readings taken during surgery. The authors note that this navigation system has previously agreed with post-operative X-rays to within 3°.

The authors conclude that the SCD method could not be applied to nearly half the X-rays and, where it could, gave values that did not match navigation. They judge it unsuitable for correcting pelvic tilt in hip replacement patients and say a more accurate correction method is still needed.

sources.abstract: Despite inaccuracies due to artifact and variations in patient positioning, anteroposterior (AP) radiographs remain the clinical standard for post-operative evaluation of component placement following total hip arthroplasty (THA). However, cup position, specifically anteversion, can be significantly affected by variations in patient positioning on an X-ray. A major cause of such artifact is unaccounted for pelvic tilt. Several methods for correcting the effects of pelvic tilt on radiographic anteversion have been proposed, with varying degrees of accuracy. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the accuracy and reliability of a commonly referenced method for correcting acetabular cup anteversion in a cohort undergoing total hip arthroplasty and determine its appropriateness for use in this population of patients. Radiographs from patients who underwent primary or revision hip arthroplasty between February 2016 and February 2017 were retrospectively reviewed. Corrected anteversion was calculated by measuring the vertical distance between the symphysis pubis and the sacrococcygeal joint, per the method outlined by Tannast et al. This symphococcygeal distance was then applied to Tannast’s nomograms to calculate the magnitude of pelvic tilt. Corrected and uncorrected anteversion values were compared to anteversion values collected intraoperatively using an imageless computer-assisted navigation device. A total of 71 cases were initially eligible for inclusion in the study. The correction method could not be applied in 44% (31/71) of the cases, chiefly due to difficulties in visualizing the required landmarks. In cases where it could be applied, corrected values correlated very poorly with navigation measurements (r = -0.07). sources.sec-introduction-1/p3: Pelvic tilt has been a subject of much discussion regarding its effect on radiographic accuracy, as variations in pelvic tilt alter the projection of the pelvis onto the two-dimensional radiograph, introducing error to the measurement of acetabular orientation [-]. To account for this projection error, several methods to correct pelvic tilt on radiographs have been presented in the literature [,], but have yet to achieve general acceptance for clinical use. [] evaluated several proposed measurements and found that the vertical distance from the pubic symphysis to the sacrococcygeal joint (symphococcygeal distance, (SCD)) correlated well with pelvic tilt. Using this method, the authors developed a nomogram for easy calculation of “tilt-corrected anteversion”. However, the broad application of their preferred method may be difficult, as their radiographic methods were highly standardized and deviate from standard clinical procedure. Furthermore, as they used a cohort of young patients, the validity of their correction method in an older population undergoing THA is in question.
sources.sec-materials-and-methods-2/p4: Anteversion was measured using the trans-ischial line method.
